newsitem.title: UK: Brent cargo trades stable, other markets quiet.
newsitem.headline: Brent cargo trades stable, other markets quiet.

text.p: Apart from two physical Brent deals no other paper or wet trade was reported in a dull start to the week.
A cargo of May 4-6 Brent was bought by a trader at June Brent -37 cents for a minimum sized cargo. Another trader picked up a May 6-8 cargo earlier at a dated related price.
"It's steady to firmer but the market doesn't seem to want to go down now. There are buyers around for most of the grades," one refiner said.
The Brent CFD market was the most actively discussed, though no trade was reported.

June Brent on the IPE lost its early strength on the back of news that Shell said it would restart normal production from Nigerian Forcados after reaching agreement with local communities to reopen oil flow stations that were shut since the end of last week.
Over the morning one trader bid this week's (Apr 28-02) Brent CFD dates at a strong June -34 cents against an offer one cent firmer.
The roll over the following three weeks was offered at evens and bid around two cents lower, brokers said.

"I was a bit surprised at the strength this morning but then again nothing got done and the dates....you could drive a bus through them," one major paper trader said refering to the quotes on the intermonth spreads.
Brent May/June was -18/-13 cents with June/July and July/Aug also wide apart at -10/-6 cents.
Forties was offered at Dated +25 cents with bids four cents lower, traders said.
Although there were no Brent cargoes on the original May Brent loading schedule for today, one cargo was brought forward early on Monday.
Another was expected to be advanced to Monday's range.
"Then there is talk of top-ups making another cargo so we could go from none to three but two (Brent cargoes) is more likely," a Brent equity holder said.
In a quiet Mediterranean market, traders said there was no Russian Urals on offer on a firm basis but there might be one or two cargoes yet to be shown in the first decade of May.

"I think people are thinking there might not be as much availability in May from Novo because there are all these maintenance programmes," a trader said referring to Russia's main Black Sea oil port, Novorossiisk.

"Also with the (Iraqi) Kirkuk looking relatively attractive, I think people are bought into that (idea) as much as possible. I am not sure how much buying interest there is going to be (for Urals)," she added.
A trader said Urals was talked unchanged to a little firmer, Dated Brent -$1.05, but the short-term outlook for the sour grade was a bit bearish.
"I think it is unchanged, reasonably firm, around (Dated Brent -)$1.05. Give it a couple of weeks, two or three weeks, and I think it will be weaker," she said.

The reasons she cited included pressure from cheaper grades like Iraqi Kirkuk and also "from going into the summer season", when demand dips for Urals, which produces less gasoline than sweeter crudes.
Another trader said Urals would probably maintain its current levels but may weaken a little not because of pressure from Kirkuk but "simply because $1 under Dated Brent for Urals is overvalued."
A trader said that although good volumes of sweet North Sea crudes have gone into the Med recently, growing tightness in the North could stem the flow.
-- H Haddadin/S Hayden, London newsroom +171 542 8145
